free-ppt.pain: You need a deck and don't want to buy a subscription
free-ppt.scene: A report, thesis defence or pitch is due. Every template site wants a membership, and design isn't your strong suit.
steps: First get the AI to turn your topic into an outline: how many sections, what each one covers. The outline matters more than the template — think it through before you start building.
Paste the outline in and it generates the whole deck, images and layout included. The Chinese UI is good if you need it.
If you want a more formal, China-style layout (corporate or teaching decks), generate it here instead — the templates fit better.
When the deck needs a flowchart or timeline, drop that paragraph in and it becomes an editable diagram. Ten times faster than dragging shapes.
free-ppt.cost_free: ¥0 all the way: Gamma gives you credits on signup, Gezhe and Napkin both have free tiers — enough for one complete deck.
free-ppt.cost_paid: Paid equivalent: template site memberships run about ¥30–100/mo; outsourcing one deck starts around ¥200.
free-ppt.tip: Get the outline right in Doubao before you generate — generator credits are limited, don't burn them re-doing the structure.
free-ppt.prompt: I need to present on X to an audience of X for X minutes. Before writing anything, ask me 3 questions as an expert to pin down what I need, then give me an outline in 3–5 sections.

free-video-edit.pain: You want to edit video but can't edit and won't pay
free-video-edit.scene: You've got footage for a short video. Pro software is too much to learn, and online tools charge for everything and still watermark it.
steps: Do the main edit here: auto-subtitles, script-to-video and the stock library are all free, and exports have no watermark.
For talking-head content built from an article, paste the text and it produces the video — the AI presenter is free too.
Already have a long video (a stream replay, a talk)? This cuts the highlights and adds vertical subtitles automatically.
When you need to split music from vocals, this does stem separation for free.
free-video-edit.cost_free: ¥0: CapCut's core and most AI features are free, Dujia is free, OpusClip grants monthly credits.
free-video-edit.cost_paid: Paid equivalent: editor subscriptions around ¥20–60/mo; auto-clipping tools from about $29/mo.
free-video-edit.tip: Finish the edit before you think about clipping it up for distribution — doing it the other way round means redoing work.
free-video-edit.prompt: Here is my video script: X. Break it into 15-second shots, and for each one note what is on screen, what the subtitle says, and how long it runs.

free-paper.pain: Research papers and literature reviews, and every tool wants a subscription
free-paper.scene: You're starting a thesis or writing a review: hundreds of papers to search, English originals to read, and the language still needs polishing. The licensed tools cost hundreds a year.
steps: Start with its academic mode for topic search — completely free, unlimited, and results carry their sources. Far cleaner than a normal search engine.
Once you have a core paper, generate its citation graph to see who cites whom and how the field is shaped.
For close reading: Chinese interface, click-to-translate, AI explanation of any paragraph. Good for getting through English originals.
When you need to compare methods and findings across many papers, this extracts them into a table automatically.
Polish the finished English for grammar and academic register.
free-paper.cost_free: ¥0 to start: Metaso is entirely free and the rest have free tiers — enough for a full round of literature research.
free-paper.cost_paid: Paid equivalent: academic search and editing subscriptions around $10–20/mo, human editing charged per word on top.
free-paper.tip: Metaso works without even logging in, so it's the lowest-friction step in the chain. Start there.
free-paper.prompt: My research area is X. List the 10 most worthwhile papers from the last 3 years, saying what problem each solves and what method it uses, and how they cite one another.

free-api-dev.pain: You want to build with AI but the API bills scare you off
free-api-dev.scene: You're an indie developer or a student with a small AI project in mind, and one look at per-token pricing kills the idea.
steps: Start here: Gemini's free tier is generous, needs no card, and covers most personal projects.

Second workhorse: the free tier has no total cap — it is rate-limited only, no card needed (official pricing-page wording), with very fast open-model inference. When you hit the limiter, switch providers.
Reliable floor: 10,000 free Neurons per day (official docs figure), resetting daily at 00:00 UTC — well suited to scheduled jobs.
One key reaches 20+ fully free models (IDs ending in :free) — handy when you want to compare models side by side.
Direct access from mainland China, sign-up credits, some small models free long-term, OpenAI-SDK compatible.
For the Qwen family: new users get a million-token grant per model.
Install this editor plugin, drop in any free key from above, and you have a zero-cost AI coding assistant.
free-api-dev.cost_free: ¥0: stack the free tiers above and a personal project will rarely hit a ceiling.
free-api-dev.cost_paid: Paid equivalent: commercial APIs bill per token; a moderate personal project runs about $10–50/mo.
free-api-dev.tip: The right way is to stack: every platform speaks the OpenAI SDK, so build a fallback list of base_urls and keys — when one rate-limits you, roll to the next. Free-tier limits are almost all about rate, not volume; stack three providers and the walls effectively disappear.
free-api-dev.prompt: I want to call the X API from Python to do X. Give me complete runnable code with error handling and retries, and explain each parameter in the comments.

free-copywriting.pain: Writing social posts and newsletters, and nothing comes out
free-copywriting.scene: You're publishing daily. Angles, headlines, body copy and images are all on you, and it grinds you down.
steps: Ask it for ten angles and headline directions on your topic, then pick. Much faster than starting from a blank page.
Run your first draft through this for Chinese polishing, rewriting and expansion — free and unmetered.
Proofread the whole piece before publishing. It catches typos and clumsy grammar better than your own eyes do.
Generate the images here — daily check-in credits, and it understands Chinese prompts well.
When you need a finished cover with text laid out, use a template here — better suited to covers than raw generation.
free-copywriting.cost_free: ¥0: Huoshan Writing is entirely free, and daily check-ins on the rest cover a daily publishing habit.
free-copywriting.cost_paid: Paid equivalent: writing assistants around ¥20–50/mo, stock image memberships ¥30–100/mo.
free-copywriting.tip: Don't have AI write the whole piece — have it generate angles and edit your drafts. AI prose reads generic, but AI editing is genuinely strong.
free-copywriting.prompt: I am writing a post about X for an audience of X. Give me 10 headline angles first, noting the emotion each one leads with; I will pick one before you write the body.

free-meeting-notes.pain: Turning meeting recordings into notes is eating your day
free-meeting-notes.scene: Several meetings a week, an hour or two of audio each, and transcribing them by hand takes most of an afternoon.
steps: Upload the recording for automatic transcription. It separates speakers and pulls out action items. Free minutes granted daily.
If your team already runs on Feishu, start Minutes inside the meeting — it transcribes live and the notes exist the moment you finish.
When the transcript is too long, hand it to this for a summary — a 2-million-character context swallows a whole meeting at once.
Keep every set of notes in this knowledge base so you can just ask it later instead of scrolling through chat history.
free-meeting-notes.cost_free: ¥0: Tingwu grants minutes daily; Kimi and Tencent ima are entirely free.
free-meeting-notes.cost_paid: Paid equivalent: transcription services about ¥1–3/hour, meeting assistants ¥30–80/mo.
free-meeting-notes.tip: Name recordings by date and topic before uploading — it saves a lot of pain when you search the knowledge base later.
free-meeting-notes.prompt: Here is the transcript: X. Organise it into three parts: what was decided; action items (who, what, by when); and what is still unresolved.
free-meeting-notes.caution: Recordings routinely contain names, client names and business information that is not public. Check whether the contents of the meeting can leave the room before uploading, and never put confidential meetings through an online transcriber.

free-ecommerce-image.pain: You run a shop, your product photos are bad, and models cost money
free-ecommerce-image.scene: A small seller's own photos have messy backgrounds. You want clean white-background shots and on-model images, but a photo shoot costs hundreds.
steps: Cut the background out first — the free tier lets you preview the result.
Purpose-built for commerce: AI product shots, virtual try-on, scene replacement. The free tier covers small batches.
Lay out listing pages and hero images here — the best library of Chinese e-commerce templates.
When resolution falls short, upscale here: fully open source, runs locally, unlimited.
free-ecommerce-image.cost_free: ¥0 to start: Upscayl is free and unlimited, the rest have free tiers.
free-ecommerce-image.cost_paid: Paid equivalent: a product shoot from ¥300; e-commerce retouching memberships ¥50–200/mo.
free-ecommerce-image.tip: Upscayl runs on your own machine, so lean on it for volume — it burns none of your online credits.
free-ecommerce-image.prompt: I sell X to customers who are X. Describe 5 hero-image scenes that suit this product, each with the background, lighting, props and the feeling it should convey.
free-ecommerce-image.caution: Do not upload photos of other people for virtual try-on. Likeness rights are the kind of thing that actually lands you in trouble.

free-english.pain: Foreign-language material is slow to read and translators cap you
free-english.scene: You need to get through docs, papers and overseas news. Translating sentence by sentence is slow, and the good translators limit characters.
steps: Install the browser extension for automatic side-by-side translation. Reading the original and the translation together beats switching back and forth.
For passages that need to be exactly right, paste them in here — noticeably better than generic machine translation, and the web version needs no account.
A China-reachable alternative; the extension also does whole-page bilingual view.
Upload an entire English PDF and ask questions in your own language; it will also produce a summary.
free-english.cost_free: ¥0: Immersive Translate can run on your own free API key without limits, and DeepL's web version needs no signup.
free-english.tip: Immersive Translate accepts your own free API key (Gemini, for example). Once it's set, the quota stops being a problem.
free-english.prompt: Translate the following, keeping technical terms in the original with the English in brackets: X. Then summarise the core point in three sentences.

free-ai-chatbot.pain: You want an AI support bot or knowledge base for yourself or your company
free-ai-chatbot.scene: You have product docs and an FAQ and want a bot that answers from them, but you can't code and have no budget.
steps: The no-code starting point: drag-and-drop builder, upload documents as a knowledge base, publish to WeChat or Feishu in one click.
When you need stronger document retrieval, use this — open source, self-hostable, and your data stays yours.
For multi-step workflows (checking stock, calling an API), this is the one. Open source and self-hostable.
Self-hosting needs a model API; wire in this free tier and it just works from China without fiddling.
free-ai-chatbot.cost_free: ¥0: Coze builds and publishes free; Dify and FastGPT are open source with no licence fee when self-hosted.
free-ai-chatbot.cost_paid: Paid equivalent: commercial support-bot platforms from ¥200–1000/mo.
free-ai-chatbot.tip: Build a working version in Coze first to prove the need. Only self-host once people are actually using it — for most cases Coze is enough.
free-ai-chatbot.prompt: I want a support bot that answers questions about X. Work out the 20 questions users are most likely to ask, how each should be answered, and what it should fall back to when it cannot answer.

free-music.pain: Your video needs music and narration, and licensed audio is expensive
free-music.scene: A video or podcast needs a soundtrack and voiceover. Commercial music licences are pricey and voice talent costs more.
steps: Describe a style and mood and it writes a complete original song with vocals. Credits granted daily.
Use this for narration: entirely free, no signup, and the output is explicitly cleared for commercial use.
When you want something warmer and more presenter-like in Chinese, switch here — a much richer voice library.
Denoise or strip vocals from the audio you end up with, free.
free-music.cost_free: ¥0: TTSMaker is free and commercially usable; Suno grants credits daily.
free-music.cost_paid: Paid equivalent: music libraries from ¥300/year, human voiceover ¥50–200/minute.
free-music.tip: Check the licence before commercial use. TTSMaker states it clearly; AI music platforms differ from one another, so read the terms first.
free-music.prompt: I need background music for a video about X, mood X, X seconds long. Write a music generation prompt covering style, instruments, tempo and mood.

free-resume.pain: Your applications get no replies and you don't want to pay for a rewrite
free-resume.scene: You're job hunting. You've revised the CV several times and still aren't sure, and professional editing runs into the hundreds.
steps: Get the format right with a free template first — plenty of CVs die on layout and machine parsing rather than content.
Give it the job description alongside your experience and ask which parts of your background don't line up with what they want.
Rewrite each bullet: turn 'responsible for X' into a statement with an outcome and a number.
For roles at international companies, use this to polish the English grammar and phrasing.
free-resume.cost_free: ¥0: both the templates and the AI rewriting have free tiers — more than enough for one revision.
free-resume.cost_paid: Paid equivalent: professional CV editing ¥200–1000 per pass.
free-resume.tip: Have the AI edit against a specific job description rather than 'improve my CV' in the abstract. One targeted version beats a generic one sent to a hundred places.
free-resume.prompt: Here is the job description: X. Here is my experience: X. Tell me which experience does not line up with what they want, how to rewrite each bullet so it leads with an outcome and a number, and what I am missing and how to handle it in interview.
free-resume.caution: Remove your phone number, ID number and address before handing the CV to an AI, and put them back afterwards.

free-build-website.pain: You want to build a site or product and can't write code
free-build-website.scene: You have an idea worth building. Agencies quote five figures and learning to code takes too long.
steps: Describe what you want in plain language in the browser and it generates a project that actually runs. Tokens granted daily.
When the app needs logins and a database, use this — it wires up the backend for you.
To keep editing the generated code, download this AI IDE and use the major models for free.
If all you need is a marketing site, design it here and publish it free.
free-build-website.cost_free: ¥0 to start: each has a daily or monthly free allowance, and an MVP usually fits inside it.
free-build-website.cost_paid: Paid equivalent: agency development from ¥5,000; low-code platforms ¥100–500/mo.
free-build-website.tip: Break the work into features you can describe in one sentence and build one at a time. Describe ten features at once and what comes back usually won't run.
free-build-website.prompt: I want to build an X site whose one core feature is X. Implement only that feature, with the simplest possible stack, and make sure the code runs as-is.

free-data-analysis.pain: You're staring at a spreadsheet with no idea how to analyse it
free-data-analysis.scene: You have sales figures or survey data and need conclusions for a presentation, but you can't write formulas, let alone code.
steps: Upload the sheet and ask in plain language which category is declining — it writes the code, runs it and draws the chart.
Write formulas and build pivot tables with AI directly inside WPS, without exporting anything.
For sheets several people work on, use this — the AI features live inside the document.
Turn your conclusions into editable diagrams; far more professional in a deck than a screenshot of raw data.
free-data-analysis.cost_free: ¥0: Zhipu Qingyan is free and the office suites' basic AI allowances cost nothing.
free-data-analysis.cost_paid: Paid equivalent: BI tools ¥100–500/mo, outsourced analysis priced per project.
free-data-analysis.tip: Clean up the headers and remove merged cells before uploading. When AI analysis goes wrong, a messy sheet structure is usually why.
free-data-analysis.prompt: Here is my spreadsheet (uploaded). First tell me what questions this data can and cannot answer, then analyse X and chart the conclusion.
free-data-analysis.caution: If the sheet contains phone numbers, ID numbers or a client list, strip or pseudonymise them first — most free AI services use your conversations for training by default.

If you only need the voice and not a face, generate the audio here and put your own visuals behind it — cheaper again.
free-digital-human.cost_free: ¥0 to start: Dujia is free and the rest all have free trial allowances.
free-digital-human.cost_paid: Paid equivalent: avatar platforms ¥100–500/mo, a custom avatar from ¥2,000.
free-digital-human.tip: Make a 30-second sample on the free tier and see whether you can live with it. AI presenters land in the uncanny valley, and not every kind of content survives that.
free-digital-human.prompt: Here is my script: X. Rewrite it for spoken delivery: shorter sentences, no written-register phrasing, nothing over 20 words a sentence, and mark where to pause.

free-study.pain: Teaching yourself something new with no idea where to start and nobody to ask
free-study.scene: You want to learn a skill or get through a subject. The material is scattered everywhere and there's no one to ask when you get stuck.
steps: Work out what the field actually consists of: search and summarise here, with sources attached so you're less likely to be led astray.
Load everything you found — PDFs, pages, videos — into a private knowledge base. It will even generate a podcast-style audio summary for your commute.
Stuck on a specific problem? Photograph it and get a step-by-step explanation, free.
Keep your notes in this knowledge base and query them directly when you revise.
free-study.cost_free: ¥0: Metaso, NotebookLM, Doubao Aixue and Tencent ima are all free to use.
free-study.cost_paid: Paid equivalent: online courses ¥200–2,000 each, one-to-one tutoring from ¥100/hour.
free-study.tip: NotebookLM answers only from the material you upload and cites where each claim came from, so it invents far less than a general chatbot. That's the reason to use it when you're learning.
free-study.prompt: I want to learn X. My current level is X and I can put in X hours a day. Give me a four-week path: what to study each week, what materials to use, and how to check I have actually learned it.

free-ask-ai.pain: You opened the AI and had no idea what to type
free-ask-ai.scene: The tools are installed, the cursor blinks in an empty box, you type something vague, the AI returns a page of correct-sounding nothing, and you give up.
steps: Don't lead with a request — make it interrogate you first: "I want to do X but I haven't fully thought it through. Ask me questions as an expert in this area until you're confident, then start." This alone solves most of the blank-box problem.

Replace vague words with checkable ones. Not "make it better" but "no paragraph over three lines, cut every adjective". Not "shorter" but "under 200 words". AI can't tell what "good" means; it can tell what a number means.
The first version is always a C. Don't start over — say "paragraph two is thin, add a concrete example". Good answers are talked into shape, not extracted in one go.
Verify anything factual separately. Drop the key claims into this search engine: its answers carry sources, which beats asking the AI "are you sure?"
free-ask-ai.cost_free: ¥0: all four are completely free and reachable from mainland China.
free-ask-ai.cost_paid: Paid equivalent: prompt-engineering courses ¥99–999, most of which are the points above stretched out.
free-ask-ai.tip: Only one rule really matters: treat the AI as a very capable new colleague who knows nothing about your situation. Give it the background, an example and what 'done' looks like — the same way you'd brief a person.
free-ask-ai.prompt: I want to do X, but I haven't fully worked it out. Ask me 3–5 questions as an expert in this field, and only start once you're confident you understand what I need.

free-homework.pain: Helping with homework and losing your mind first
free-homework.scene: You can't parse the question, you've explained it three times and it still hasn't landed, and tutoring costs a few hundred an hour. It's 10pm and you're still at the desk.
steps: Photograph the question and it walks through the reasoning rather than just handing over an answer. Let your child read the explanation while you check the logic holds.
When it doesn't land, ask the AI to switch registers: "Explain that again in language a fourth-grader would follow, with an example from everyday life."
For knowledge questions (history, science), verify here — the results carry sources, so an AI mistake doesn't slip past you.
Store the questions your child keeps getting wrong in a knowledge base, then ask before an exam which kind of problem trips them up most. Faster than leafing through a mistake notebook.
free-homework.cost_free: ¥0: Doubao Aixue, Doubao, Metaso and Tencent ima are all free and reachable from mainland China.
free-homework.cost_paid: Paid equivalent: one-to-one tutoring ¥150–400/hour; homework app memberships ¥30–100/mo.
free-homework.tip: Don't let your child copy the AI's answer — that's worse than not doing the homework. Have the AI explain the approach, let the child write it, then have the AI check where it went wrong.
free-homework.prompt: My child is stuck on this question (photo attached). Don't give the answer first — explain the reasoning in language a Year X student would follow, with one everyday example, and only then give the answer so we can check against it.
free-homework.caution: Crop out names, schools and class numbers before photographing homework — whatever is in the frame gets uploaded with it.

free-life.pain: Deciding what to eat and what to buy is more tiring than work
free-life.scene: You can't think what's for dinner on the way home, the vegetables in the fridge keep going off, weekend shopping has no plan, and takeaway keeps getting more expensive.
steps: Photograph or list what's already in the fridge and have it plan a week of dinners on a use-it-up basis, working out what's still missing.
Turn that week's plan into a shopping list grouped by supermarket aisle (produce, meat, condiments) so you're not walking back and forth.
Take a photo when it's done and generate a nicer-looking version — useful for sharing or just keeping a record.
Record what your family likes and won't eat in a knowledge base, then just say "plan a week for my household" without re-explaining every time.
free-life.cost_free: ¥0: Doubao, Kimi and Tencent ima are free; Jimeng grants credits on daily check-in.
free-life.cost_paid: Paid equivalent: a nutritionist's meal plan ¥200–1,000/mo, recipe app memberships ¥20–60/mo.
free-life.tip: Ask it to plan around using up what you already have, not to recommend recipes from scratch. The first genuinely saves money; the second just makes you buy more.
free-life.prompt: My fridge currently has: X. There are X of us and one person doesn't eat spicy food. Plan a week of dinners on a use-up-what-we-have basis, noting what to cook each day and roughly how long it takes, then give me a shopping list for what's missing, grouped by supermarket aisle.

free-read-doc.pain: Medical results, contracts and manuals you can't make sense of
free-read-doc.scene: Test results are all arrows and abbreviations, contracts run to a dozen dense pages, and you've read the insurance terms three times and still don't know if you're covered. Asking someone feels like an imposition; not asking leaves you uneasy.
steps: Upload the whole document and start with "how many separate things does this cover — give me one plain sentence for each". Get the shape first, then dig in.
Go through the confusing parts one by one: "if this clause worked against me, what would that look like in practice? Give a concrete example." Far more useful than asking what it means.
For technical measures or legal wording, verify the AI's account here — the results carry sources so you can see the original basis.
When you have several documents to compare (competing insurance terms, say), load them all in. It answers only from your files and cites which one, so it invents far less.
free-read-doc.cost_free: ¥0: Kimi, Doubao and Metaso are free; NotebookLM is free but needs access outside mainland China.
free-read-doc.cost_paid: Paid equivalent: a lawyer reviewing a contract ¥300–2,000; a health consultation ¥100–500.
free-read-doc.tip: AI can help you understand it; it can't decide for you. Abnormal test results still mean seeing a doctor, and a contract that matters still means a lawyer. Treat it as a translator for what the other side is saying, not as an adviser.
free-read-doc.caution: Medical results carry your name and ID number; contracts carry both parties' details and the amounts. Mask or remove those before uploading — most free AI services use your conversations for training by default, and some platforms retain logs for up to 180 days.
free-read-doc.prompt: This is a X (uploaded). Work through it in three steps: first, in plain language, how many separate things does this document cover; second, point out the clauses that work against me or need care, each with a concrete example of what would happen; third, list what I should still go back and confirm with the other side.

free-antifraud.pain: The face and the voice are my relative — but I am not sure it is really them
free-antifraud.scene: A video call from a "relative" needing money; a voice note from your "boss" asking for a transfer. A face and a voice can be cloned from about fifteen seconds of material, and the eye can barely tell.
steps: Save the suspect screenshot, video or audio and run it through the official AI-content check first. Ten free checks a day is plenty.
Have AI draft a list of "only we would know" verification questions for you and your family, and keep it in your phone notes. You will not have time to invent one in the moment.
If you recorded the call, transcribe it — a scam script is far more obvious as text than as a voice.
Search the organisation, the case and the account number they quoted. Real institutions do not push you to transfer within minutes.
free-antifraud.cost_free: ¥0: the official AI-content check is free, and everything else runs on free tiers already listed here.
free-antifraud.cost_paid: The cost of skipping this is not a subscription — reported single losses to face-swap scams run into tens of thousands.
free-antifraud.tip: Detection is only the second line. The first is always these three: ask them to **turn their head quickly or cover part of their face** (synthetic video tends to break down there), **ask something only the two of you know**, and **hang up and call back on the number saved in your own contacts**. Any one of the three defeats most face-swap scams.
free-antifraud.prompt: I want to agree a set of anti-deepfake verification questions with my family. Give me 8 questions where the answer is known only within our household, cannot be found on social media, involves no ID or bank card numbers, and is short enough to ask in a few seconds under pressure.
free-antifraud.caution: Do not upload family members’ clear face photos or full voice recordings to unknown sites — that is exactly where cloning material comes from. Use the official app, not third-party mini-programs.

free-interview.pain: My CV gets through, then the follow-up questions sink me
free-interview.scene: The project story goes fine until the interviewer digs two levels deeper. There is nobody to practise with, and mock-interview services run into the hundreds.
steps: Give it the job description and your experience and have it play the interviewer, **pushing three follow-ups deep on every question** instead of moving on after one answer.
Answer out loud and transcribe it. Most people have no idea how long-winded they are until they read it back.
Rewrite the transcript as situation-task-action-result, and make the result a number someone could check.
Read up on what the company has done in the past year and prepare "why us". Fumble that one and the rest stops mattering.
free-interview.cost_free: ¥0: chat, transcription, rewriting and search all run on free tiers already listed here.
free-interview.cost_paid: Paid equivalent: mock interviews and coaching at ¥200–800 a session.
free-interview.tip: Do not let the AI fire ten questions at you — that is a written test, not an interview. The damage in a real interview comes from **the follow-up**: dig three levels into one question and you find out which parts you rehearsed and which you actually did.
free-interview.prompt: You are interviewing me for the role of X, and your style is relentless. Rules: ask one question at a time; after each answer you must follow up on what I actually said, three levels deep, before moving on; if an answer is vague or has no numbers, say so. Start with the X project on my CV.
free-interview.caution: Do not feed a previous employer’s client names, internal figures or unannounced projects into AI. Practise with "an e-commerce client" instead — it works just as well.

free-elders.pain: I want to teach my parents to use AI, but "I will never learn this" ends it
free-elders.scene: You know it could help them read a label, understand a health report, or spot a scam. Two attempts later they have given up — not because they cannot learn it, but because they are afraid to touch it.
steps: **Start with voice, not typing.** Far more older learners stall on the keyboard than on the idea. Hold to speak, release, get an answer — they should feel that on the very first try.
Teach scam protection second, not last. Their biggest worry is being cheated; clear that and the rest goes in.
Pick one thing they actually want solved — a health report, a label, a birthday message. Teach the specific task, never "what AI is".
Save the good answers somewhere they can re-read. They will not want to keep asking you, and being able to look it up again matters more than you think.
free-elders.cost_free: ¥0: voice chat, transcription and the notebook all run on free tiers already listed here.
free-elders.cost_paid: Paid equivalent: smartphone classes for seniors at ¥99–500 a course.
free-elders.tip: The most counter-intuitive finding in the research: **the barrier is psychological, not technical** — fear of pressing the wrong thing, of not learning it, of looking slow in front of family. So teach one thing at a time, then have them do the whole thing themselves while you keep your hands off. One success beats ten explanations.
free-elders.prompt: I am teaching an older relative who is not confident with smartphones to do X with AI. Break it into at most 5 steps, one sentence each, in the plainest spoken language, with no English and no jargon; after each step add one line describing what they should see, so they can check they got it right.
free-elders.caution: Agree one rule before you start: **never photograph and upload an ID card, bank card or home address** — to any tool at all. That matters more than any feature you teach.

free-video-gen.pain: Free AI video generation — ideally without the watermark
free-video-gen.scene: Creators and students search "free AI video generator" and find guides that contradict each other; in practice everything is either out of credits or watermarked.
steps: Daily workhorse: logging in grants 66 credits a day — roughly 6 standard-mode 5-second videos, a figure confirmed in the official membership plan.
For extra takes, switch to Off-Peak mode: it generates without spending credits at all, as stated on the official pricing page — ideal for unhurried batch experiments.
Backup line: free and open to use but queued, about 5 seconds per clip at 1440×960, with a watermark; membership at ¥19/month removes it and adds priority.
Best for effect templates: 30–60 credits granted daily (official blog figure — the in-app dashboard is authoritative). Free output is watermarked and personal, non-commercial only.
Pull your clips into CapCut/Jianying for editing, subtitles and music — basic editing and smart subtitles are free, so don't burn generation credits on full-length cuts.
free-video-gen.cost_free: ¥0 end to end: stack the daily and monthly free quotas and you can reliably produce a few 5-second clips a day. Honest caveat: free-tier output is almost always watermarked — the watermark is exactly where vendors draw the free/paid line.
free-video-gen.cost_paid: Paid reference: video-generation memberships run about ¥19–100/month (e.g. Qingying membership at ¥19/month removes the watermark and adds priority).
free-video-gen.tip: Every guide claiming "completely free, unlimited, no watermark" failed our official-source check — all of them. Use free tiers to validate scripts and storyboards; spend the smallest possible amount to de-watermark only the take worth publishing.
free-video-gen.prompt: I want a X-second short video about "XX". First break it into 3–5 shots of ≤5 seconds each; give each shot one text-to-video prompt (subject + camera move + lighting), and flag which shot is most worth spending credits on.

free-voiceover.pain: Voiceovers for videos — free, but safe for commercial use
free-voiceover.scene: Creators searching "free AI voice" find tools that all claim commercial rights — while real court rulings on AI voice infringement already exist. Publishing without reading the terms is stepping on a rake.
steps: Commercial workhorse: the free tier covers 20,000 characters a week, some voices are unlimited — and an official Commercial License Terms page states in writing that free output may be used commercially. Vanishingly rare among free TTS tools.
Mainland-China pick: iFLYTEK's voices suit Chinese narration. Note that commercial licensing differs per voice — confirm the licence scope of your chosen voice before publishing.

Best audio quality, samples only: the free tier explicitly excludes commercial rights and public use requires attribution (stated on the official pricing page). Use it to benchmark quality — never in a monetised video.
Full control via open source: the model is open and self-hostable, with the commercial boundary set by the model licence itself — right for technical teams with long-term volume.
free-voiceover.cost_free: ¥0 end to end: TTSMaker's 20,000 weekly characters covers roughly 40–60 short-video scripts, and unlimited voices remove the wall entirely.
free-voiceover.cost_paid: Paid reference: commercial voiceover memberships run about ¥30–100/month; human voiceover starts around ¥50 per clip.
free-voiceover.tip: "Free" and "licensed for commercial use" are different things — the latter is a terms question, not a tech question. ElevenLabs' free tier forbids commercial use; TTSMaker's explicitly allows it. Same "free", opposite terms. Check each vendor's official terms before publishing; never trust a guide's one-liner.
free-voiceover.prompt: Write a spoken-style script for a short video about "XX", X seconds long (about X words). Use conversational language and short sentences, put a hook in the first 3 seconds, and mark suggested pacing and pauses after the script.

free-coding-pipeline.pain: You want a complete AI coding pipeline that costs nothing — not a scattered pile of single tools
free-coding-pipeline.scene: From a one-line requirement to something live on the web, without paying: write the spec, generate the code, review it, deploy it, then work out how many rounds a day this chain can actually run. What each step hands to the next is written into the flow.
steps: **Step 1 - produce the spec.** Expand a one-line requirement into something executable: what it must do, what it must not do, and the acceptance criteria. Write it straight from the command line and save it as a spec file.

**Step 2 - write code against the spec.** Hand spec.md to Cline and let it work to the acceptance criteria. The extension itself is free and uses your own key, so this step costs exactly what your chosen key costs.
**Fuel for step 2.** Cline needs a key. Groq's free tier caps rate rather than total volume and needs no card, which suits the short, many-round edit loop; when it throttles, switch rather than wait.
**Step 3 - review.** Bring in a different model to read the same diff — one model both writing and grading its own work is marking its own homework. Free usage is rate-tiered per model.
**Step 4 - deploy and serve.** Ship it; if the app itself calls a model, Workers AI gives 10,000 Neurons a day free and is the only genuinely hosted link in this chain.

**Backup fuel.** Switch here when any step's key hits its wall — one key reaches 20+ zero-dollar models. Note it has its own 50-requests-a-day ceiling, making it one of the tightest links in the chain.
free-coding-pipeline.cost_free: Zero throughout. But be clear that the chain is not unlimited: each step's ceiling is expressed in a different unit (requests per day, Neurons per day, per-minute rate), and this page lists the verified ceilings side by side without converting between them — a conversion would need an official basis the vendors do not publish, and it cannot be invented.
free-coding-pipeline.cost_paid: For comparison, the paid equivalent runs about $10-20 per seat per month for a commercial coding assistant, plus metered API spend.
free-coding-pipeline.tip: The real bottleneck in this chain is almost always the fuel step rather than the editor: editor-side tools are mostly open source with no allowance at all, and what hits a wall is the key you put into them.
free-coding-pipeline.prompt: I want to build <one-line requirement>. Output only the spec first: goal, non-goals, acceptance criteria - no code yet.

kimi.name: Kimi (Moonshot AI)
kimi.tagline: Very long context — built for reading long documents
kimi.free: Web and app are free, with a 2-million-character context window and document parsing.
kimi.how: Sign up with a phone number on the site or in the app.

The free tier has an official name in Kimi's membership system — **Adagio** — above which sit Andante (¥49) and Moderato (¥99). Value-added features (deep research, PPT, code) require membership quota, and since they share one pool, using any of them spends the same allowance. You can check what's left: avatar at bottom-left → Settings → Subscription shows the remaining balance as a percentage, the next refresh time, and your last 1,000 usage records — unusual transparency for a chat product that publishes no fixed message count.

"Unlimited" also carries two stated boundaries: it is **text only** — limits on file uploads, images and other tools still apply — and it is explicitly **subject to abuse guardrails**. The earlier position still holds for everything non-text: OpenAI's Help Center states plainly that free-tier model usage is limited without publishing a message count, and the official line is that ChatGPT tells you when you hit the cap and when it resets. Logged-out users can't reach the newest flagship model. Every "X messages per Y hours" figure circulating online has no official source.

OpenAI also notes that the default model and available limits change over time — which is exactly why we don't pin a number, and the 2026-08-06 change is a footnote to that sentence. **The wall has moved rather than vanished**: OpenAI says the text-chat wall is gone, leaving the remaining walls on file uploads, images and tool calls — none of which it publishes figures for either. For contrast on the paid side: Plus and Pro users get the more reliable GPT-5.6 Sol and a slider for how much thinking goes into an answer, while Go (officially $8/month) gets Luna and unlimited text just like the free tier.

ai-tool-review-account.title: Run an AI tool review account
ai-tool-review-account.who: Anyone who can carve out an hour a day and is willing to be on camera — or at least record their screen and talk over it. No technical background needed.
ai-tool-review-account.why: One of the paths the research kept confirming. A concrete case: a Douyin account testing one AI tool a day in 1–3 minute videos grew to 500k followers. The reason is plain — new tools ship every day, ordinary people have no time to try them all, so you try them instead.
steps: Lock a narrow angle before you open the account. Not 'AI tool reviews' but 'AI tools for primary school teachers' or 'AI tools for e-commerce sellers'. Broad accounts lose to the big ones; narrow accounts get watched.

Take your topics straight from the tool library here, one a day. Your script only has to answer three things: what problem it solves, where the free tier stops, and when not to use it. The third one is the most liked and the least done.
Screen recording plus voiceover — you never have to be on camera. Editing and subtitles are covered end to end by free tools.
After publishing, rewrite the same piece as a text-and-image post and publish it again — video and text audiences barely overlap, so one extra channel roughly doubles your reach.
ai-tool-review-account.first_week: What week one can actually finish: pick the angle, open the account, publish five posts. That is verifiable progress, and it has nothing to do with follower count.
ai-tool-review-account.reality: Most people die in week two: seven or eight posts land with no reaction and they stop. This path is fundamentally 'daily posting traded for algorithmic trust', and the first 30 posts return almost nothing — that is not you doing badly, that is the rule of the game. If you cannot get through 30 posts, don't start; you will only waste the time.
traps: People will sell you 'a ready-made high-authority account'. Most are repost farms that get throttled the moment you publish something original, and the money is gone.
Don't buy an 'AI asset pack'. The material inside is duplicated all over the internet, and using it invites copyright complaints.
ai-tool-review-account.cost: ¥0: the tools you review are the free ones listed here, editing in CapCut, images in Jimeng.

ai-copywriting-service.title: Write product descriptions and detail pages for small sellers
ai-copywriting-service.who: Anyone whose writing is decent and who can stand going back and forth with clients. No design or e-commerce background needed.
ai-copywriting-service.why: One of the three main paths the research verified. It works because small sellers cannot write a decent product description themselves, yet hiring a copywriter does not pencil out — that middle ground has been empty all along. And it happens to be exactly the kind of work AI can carry 70% of.
steps: Build three samples first. Pick any three real products and write their detail-page copy your way — nobody hands a first job to someone with no samples.

Run every job through the same routine: pin down the selling points and target buyer → have AI produce five angles → you pick one and rewrite it → proofread. AI drafts, you judge which angle is right. That judgement is the 30% that is yours.
Do the images while you are at it — it lifts your rate noticeably, because what the client wants is something ready to use, not a block of text.
List the service on Xianyu, Xiaohongshu and local merchant groups. Start cheap to collect your first five reviews, then raise the price.
ai-copywriting-service.first_week: What week one can finish: three samples plus a listed service. When the first order arrives depends on where you listed it and who saw it, and that is not something we can promise you.
ai-copywriting-service.reality: Most people freeze at quoting. Too low and you work yourself into the ground; too high and nobody orders. The practical fix: treat the first five orders as buying reviews, tell the client plainly that this price is for the first five only, then raise it on the strength of those reviews — that way your own low price does not trap you.
traps: Be wary of training that guarantees you orders. The research records it explicitly: orders are promised, the real rate turns out to be ¥20–30 a piece, and the agency then goes dark.
Do not take deliver-first-pay-later work. Not getting paid after delivery is the classic hazard here, especially on large jobs from strangers.
ai-copywriting-service.cost: ¥0: writing, proofreading and images all use free tools listed here.

ai-chatbot-for-smb.title: Build an AI support bot for a local business
ai-chatbot-for-smb.who: Anyone willing to tinker with tools and explain things to a shop owner in plain language. No coding required.
ai-chatbot-for-smb.why: The research puts a single project at ¥8k–30k, the highest ticket of any path here. It works because a small business owner is asked the same handful of questions dozens of times a day — hours, address, prices, refunds — while hiring someone to answer them is not worth it, and no-code tools can now do the job.
steps: Build one for yourself first. Pick a shop you know well — your family's, a friend's — and write its common questions into a document.
Assemble it on a no-code platform, publish it to WeChat, and let the owner actually use it for a few days. Having something to demo beats any pitch.
Take that demo to a second shop. Do not talk about AI — ask how many times a day people ask what time they close. That is what the owner cares about.
Charge a maintenance fee after delivery. Menus, prices and promotions all change, and that is the only reliable repeat revenue on this path.
ai-chatbot-for-smb.first_week: What week one can finish: one shop with a working, demoable bot. That is the only real barrier on this path — everything after it repeats.
ai-chatbot-for-smb.reality: Most people stall at not being able to find the first customer. The real fix is not cold outreach, it is starting with people you already know — the shop downstairs, a friend's studio. This path runs on trust, not scripts. Also, do not overestimate automation: AI handles common questions, not disputes, and you must spell that boundary out to the owner or the fallout lands on you.
traps: Never promise a fully automatic, unattended system. When a real complaint blows up, it is yours.
Do not start on a platform that charges before you can publish — validate demand on a free one, and discuss upgrades only once the client is sold.
ai-chatbot-for-smb.cost: ¥0: build and publish free on Coze, knowledge base in Tencent ima, model credits from free tiers.

ai-teaching-elders.title: Teach people who can't use AI how to use AI
ai-teaching-elders.who: Patient people who explain things clearly. Knowing slightly more than the other person is enough.
ai-teaching-elders.why: The most underrated finding in the research: over 90% of ordinary people cannot use AI, and the blocker is not knowing what to say rather than not having a tool. Almost nobody is seriously filling that gap — everyone teaches advanced tricks and nobody teaches people how to open their mouth.
steps: Work through this site's recipes yourself first. What you teach is not what AI is, it is how to finish this specific task with AI.

Lock one kind of person and one task — teaching shop owners to write social posts with AI, say, or teaching parents to use AI on homework. The narrower it is, the easier to teach and the easier to charge for.

Walk three people through it for free first and write down every place they got stuck. Those blockers are the entire content of whatever you build later, and far more accurate than guessing at your desk.
Start one-on-one or with a tiny group; do not open with a recorded course. Recorded courses need traffic, one-on-one only needs word of mouth.
ai-teaching-elders.first_week: What week one can finish: run three recipes yourself, and find three people willing to be walked through them for free.
ai-teaching-elders.reality: Most people overestimate how much they need to know before they can teach. To teach ordinary people AI, being three months ahead of them is enough. The real difficulty is patience: still explaining the same question well the third time — that is the actual barrier here. And one more thing: **what you teach is something they could learn free elsewhere; what you charge for is walking beside them, so do not package yourself as a guru**, because that road ends at selling courses.
traps: Do not build a course that promises five figures a month. The research records it plainly: the content of those courses is all freely available online, and once students find out it becomes complaints and refunds.

Do not use instalment-payment tactics. One consumer was pushed into a ¥6,000 instalment plan they then could not cancel — one of the ugliest practices in this industry, and doing it ends any word of mouth you had.
ai-teaching-elders.cost: ¥0: the teaching material is this site's recipes; the only thing you invest is time.

ai-content-account.title: Run a niche content account and take sponsorships
ai-content-account.who: People genuinely interested in some subject who can keep publishing. Interest is the only fuel that lasts on this path.
ai-content-account.why: A common route in the research: niche content plus sponsorships. It works because advertisers are looking for small accounts that are precise and trusted, not big ones — niche accounts often convert better, which is why someone is willing to pay.
steps: Pick a narrow field you were already interested in. A field you do not care about will not survive three months, and that is not a willpower problem.
Use AI for angles and first drafts; you make it sound human. Platforms can tell AI writing and readers do not warm to it — its value is moving you from can't-write to just-editing.
Do images and covers entirely with free tools. The cover decides the click-through rate, so it deserves the extra time.
Advertisers come to you once you have a few thousand followers. Before that, make what this account is about unmistakable — nobody sponsors a vague account.
ai-content-account.first_week: What week one can finish: pick the angle, publish the first five posts, write a clear bio.
ai-content-account.reality: This is the slowest path and the easiest to abandon. The honest picture is that the first three months return essentially nothing, and most people quit around post 20. If you are going to do it, accept up front that the first 50 posts are tuition — and if you cannot accept that, take one of the faster paths above.
traps: Do not buy followers. Bought followers do not engage, the account gets flagged as anomalous, and an advertiser sees it in the numbers at a glance.
Do not take sponsorships unrelated to what the account is about. One bad fit can destroy trust you spent six months building.
ai-content-account.cost: ¥0: writing, images and layout all use free tools listed here.

ai-design-service.title: Take small AI-assisted design jobs
ai-design-service.who: People with some taste who are willing to learn the basic tools. No formal design training needed.
ai-design-service.why: One of the three main paths the research verified. It works because small merchants do not need fine design — they need usable, cheap and fast. Posters, covers and product images are high in volume and low in price, which is exactly the slice AI assistance can take.
steps: Make 10 pieces and have them ready. No portfolio, no jobs — this trade judges with the eyes, not the mouth.
One template tool is enough to start. Most small jobs are template-plus-new-text, not creation from scratch.
Use a dedicated tool for product-image jobs; it is far faster than a general-purpose one.
List your work on Xianyu and Xiaohongshu. State exactly how many revisions are included, or you will be dragged to death by endless changes.
ai-design-service.first_week: What week one can finish: 10 pieces, a listed service, and a written cap on revisions.
ai-design-service.reality: Most people are wrecked by unlimited revisions. Write the revision count and the overage rate into the deal before you accept it — nearly all the pain in this trade comes from that one line. And the rates really are low; what pays is speed once you are fluent, not the price per job.
traps: Do not take let-me-see-it-first-and-I-will-pay-if-I-like-it jobs. Ten revisions later they say they are not satisfied and disappear — the classic experience in this trade.
Confirm commercial licensing. Commercial terms for AI-generated images differ by platform, so check before you use them, not after a complaint arrives.
ai-design-service.cost: ¥0: generation, templates and background removal all use free tools listed here.

traps: "Free" almost always means the collection exhibitions only — special exhibitions run on separate tickets, the norm across Tokyo's major museums.
Of the three free days, Respect-for-the-Aged Day is a moving date (21 September in 2026) — check the current year's official notice before building an itinerary around it.
tokyo.tip: The best play in Tokyo is to land on one of the three free days, or travel with someone under 18 or over 70 — the collection exhibitions then cost nothing, leaving the budget for the special exhibition you actually came for.

seoul.lede: Same rule: official sources only. Seoul's National Museum of Korea is among the most generous "permanent collection is free" cases anywhere — but its closing-day rules are unusual enough to check first.

free.name: National Museum of Korea
free.policy: The permanent exhibition halls are free, as are the Children's Museum and some special exhibitions. Permanent halls open 9:30–17:30 (closed 12:00–13:00); last admission is 30 minutes before closing, with visitors guided out 10 minutes before.
free.wall: Free covers the permanent halls and free special exhibitions; ticketed special exhibitions are extra. **The closing days are the catch**: 1 January, Lunar New Year, the Chuseok holiday, and the first Monday of March, June, September and December; the permanent halls also close on the first Monday of April and November — planning around "closed Mondays" will misfire.
free.source: National Museum of Korea official English visitor information (museum.go.kr, verified via search-index quotes)

free.name: Outdoor exhibition area and Pagoda Garden
free.policy: The outdoor exhibition area is open 07:00–22:00 and the Pagoda Garden needs no ticket.
free.wall: The outdoor areas aren't affected by the midday closure of the indoor halls — early morning and evening both work.
free.source: National Museum of Korea official English visitor information (museum.go.kr, verified via search-index quotes)

traps: Don't assume "closed on Mondays": here it's the first Monday of specific months (March, June, September, December for the whole museum; April and November for the permanent halls). Other Mondays are open.
The permanent halls close between 12:00 and 13:00 — arriving at noon means an hour of waiting.
seoul.tip: Seoul costs almost nothing: the permanent collection is free and the outdoor area stays open until 10 pm. The only homework is checking whether the month's first Monday is a closing day, and avoiding the 12:00–13:00 indoor closure.
